chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: In this video we are going to cover classes in python, which is one of those topics that

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: can get really difficult for beginners. So let's approach this slowly.

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: Most importantly, classes are a way to organize your code. They don't really allow you to do

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: new things, instead they are there to better organize what you already have.

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: For an example, imagine you want to make some kind of game with multiple characters,

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: like mages, monsters, traders, lots of other classes, doesn't really matter for the example.

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: Each character is going to have unique attributes and abilities. For example the mage has health,

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: mana and weapons, those would be attributes. And cast magic would be a method, i.e. a function.

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: For a monster, we might just have health along with an attack method. All of that information

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: could be stored in a list or in a dictionary, but it would kind of be a nightmare to work with.

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: The result might look something like this, where you have one extensive character dictionary,

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: that contains a mage with a dictionary and then a monster, and afterwards you would have lots of

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: other characters. This would generally be possible, but this would not be fun to work with at all.

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: Also it would be kind of a pain to get functions in there. Using classes for all of that is going

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: to be much easier. For example, via classes we could create a mage object. And inside of this

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: mage object we could access mage.health and mage.mana. Also if we wanted to call a method,

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: we could simply call mage.attack and then we get some kind of output. We could even add arguments

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: inside of this method, this would work like any other method in python. We could actually add

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: even more things in there, but let's get started with the basics of a class. For that, back inside

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: of VS Code, I want to create a new file, which I'm going to call classes.py. And after that,

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: let's start with a really basic example. I want to create a basic class. For that you have to start

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: with the class keyword. And then you have to give your class a name. The naming convention for that

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: diverges a bit from what you have usually seen. For example, for a function you would have

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: word like normal. Let's say I want to call this class. And then if we want to go to the next word,

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: we don't have a space. Instead, the next word starts with an uppercase letter once again.

chunks.text: Last name like this would be a perfectly valid Python name. Although in my case, I want to call

chunks.text: this test.las. Also notice here, these are just conventions. Both would work perfectly fine,

chunks.text: but it's not usually what you see. After that, you need a double colon. And then we can write

chunks.text: function in the class. The reason why you need this self, and by the way, you could call it

chunks.text: the way this is used, is as a way to access the class itself, or more specifically,

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: the class, and 1, 2, 3. Effectively, this self is the internal equivalent to this test2 from

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: to via the parameter. If you change the name of this, it would be called something else.

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: So just to recap, self refers to any instance of the class, and must be the first parameter

chunks.text: for all methods. With that system, you can target attributes everywhere inside of the class.

chunks.text: I suppose I should demonstrate this. Let's create define another function.

chunks.title: Classes
chunks.text: underscore. For example, one really common danda method is called danda init, which is run when
